To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

droplets or bubbles produced by flow focusing in a microfluidics T junction are governed by capillary number, and that the dominant contribution of the capillary number arises from the pressure loss due to viscous dissipation in the films separating the droplets from the channel walls.

the dominant contribution in the dynamics of droplet and bubble formation at low capillary numbers is due to pressure drop in the thin liquid film between the droplet and the walls, and that this pressure drop results from flow resistance of the continuous phase in the thin liquid films.

the formation of droplets or bubbles in a microchannel T junction at low capillary number is dominated by the pressure drop across a droplet or bubble that fills the entire cross section and that the droplet or bubble diameter is determined by the balance of the pressure drop and the capillary pressure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation of droplets in a microchannel.
the formation of drops and bubbles in microchannels.

the development of microfluidic devices for the synthesis and manipulation of droplets, bubbles, and other microscale objects, as well as with the development of new methods for studying the dynamics of fluid-fluid and liquid-gas interfaces.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the formation of droplets is a result of the interplay of two competing effects: the viscous stresses in the continuous phase that tend to elongate the emerging droplet and the capillary pressure drop across the droplet that tends to pinch off the emerging droplet.
the formation of droplets in microfluidic devices is a complex process involving the interplay of many factors.

droplet formation at a T junction occurs as a result of the combined effect of the pressure drop across a droplet, which is a consequence of the resistance of the thin film separating the droplet from a wall of the channel, and the shear stress exerted by the continuous phase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the droplet or bubble size scales with the square root of the interfacial energy, and the inverse of the square root of capillary number.
the droplet or bubble size is determined by the pressure drop that occurs across the emerging droplets or bubbles.

the formation and break up of droplets and/or bubbles in microfluidics is a complex phenomenon, which depends strongly on the flow rate, the viscosity, the interfacially tension, the channel dimensions, and other factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
at low capillary numbers the dominant contribution to break up arises from a pressure drop across the thin films that separates the droplet from channel walls.
at low capillary numbers droplet and bubble sizes can be accurately predicted using a simple scaling relation.
the pressure drop across a growing droplet or bubble is the key factor that determines the size of the emerging droplets and bubbles.
